title: Greeting an Older Relative
summary: Greet an older relative on arrival

content.title: Greeting an Older Relative

chunks.note: Standard respectful greeting to a woman of your parent's generation.
Placed at the end to show respect to someone older.

rounds.situation: You arrive at your aunt's house and greet her politely.
rounds.vietnamese: Cháu chào cô ạ.
rounds.translation: Hello, Auntie.
rounds.speakingPrompt: Say aloud: Hello, Auntie.

chunks.note: Used to say you got here moments ago.
Adding 'ạ' keeps the tone respectful with elders.

rounds.situation: Your aunt asks when you arrived, and you reply respectfully.
rounds.vietnamese: Cháu vừa đến ạ.
rounds.translation: I just arrived.
rounds.speakingPrompt: Say aloud: I just arrived.

chunks.note: A common welcoming phrase when someone arrives.
A standard hospitable offer in Vietnamese homes.
'Đi' softens the invitation; 'cháu' addresses the younger person.

rounds.situation: Your aunt invites you inside to rest after your trip.
rounds.vietnamese: Vào nhà uống nước đi cháu.
rounds.translation: Come into the house and drink some water, dear.
rounds.speakingPrompt: Say aloud: Come into the house and drink some water, dear.

chunks.note: Respectful way to agree or acknowledge an elder's words.
Combines thanks with the correct address term.

rounds.situation: You thank your aunt as you step inside.
rounds.vietnamese: Vâng, cháu cảm ơn cô.
rounds.translation: Yes, thank you, Auntie.
rounds.speakingPrompt: Say aloud: Yes, thank you, Auntie.

chunks.note: Using the correct address term makes it natural and affectionate.
The standard way to ask about someone's health or state.

rounds.situation: Your aunt asks how you are doing today.

rounds.translation: Are you well?
rounds.speakingPrompt: Say aloud: Are you well?

options.englishTranslation: Are you well?

title: Asking How a Relative Is Doing
summary: Ask how a relative is doing

content.title: Asking How a Relative Is Doing

chunks.note: Used to get the attention of your father's younger brother.
A standard way to ask an older male relative about his health.

rounds.situation: You greet your father's younger brother at his house and ask how he is doing.
rounds.vietnamese: Chú ơi, chú khỏe không?
rounds.translation: Uncle, are you well?
rounds.speakingPrompt: Say aloud: Ask your uncle if he is well.

chunks.note: He uses 'chú' to refer to himself when speaking to you.
He addresses you as 'cháu' because you are his nephew or niece.

rounds.situation: Your uncle replies that he is fine and thanks you for asking.
rounds.vietnamese: Chú khỏe, cảm ơn cháu.
rounds.translation: I am well, thank you, nephew.
rounds.speakingPrompt: Say aloud: Repeat your uncle's reply thanking you.

chunks.note: 'Thế' links this question naturally to the previous topic.
Adding 'ạ' shows respect to your older uncle.

rounds.situation: You follow up by asking about your aunt's health.
rounds.vietnamese: Thế cô có khỏe không ạ?
rounds.translation: And is aunt well?
rounds.speakingPrompt: Say aloud: Ask your uncle if your aunt is also well.

options.englishTranslation: Where is aunt going?
Is aunt eating now?
And is aunt well?

responseExercise.promptVietnamese: Thế cô có khỏe không ạ?
responseExercise.promptTranslation: And is aunt well?

chunks.note: 'Cũng' means 'also', reusing the word 'khỏe' from earlier.
'Lắm' adds emphasis, meaning 'very' or 'a lot'.

rounds.situation: Your uncle answers that your aunt is also doing very well.
rounds.vietnamese: Cô cũng khỏe lắm.
rounds.translation: Aunt is also very well.
rounds.speakingPrompt: Say aloud: Repeat what your uncle says about your aunt.

chunks.note: A respectful way to say yes to an older person in Northern Vietnam.
You use 'cháu' for yourself; 'quá' means 'so' or 'very'.

rounds.situation: You express happiness that both of them are healthy.
rounds.vietnamese: Vâng, cháu mừng quá.
rounds.translation: Yes, I am so glad.
rounds.speakingPrompt: Say aloud: Tell your uncle you are very glad they are well.

options.englishTranslation: Yes, I am leaving now.
Yes, I am so glad.
Yes, I am very tired.

responseExercise.promptVietnamese: Vâng, cháu mừng quá.
responseExercise.promptTranslation: Yes, I am so glad.

content.title: Changing the family dinner plan

chunks.note: 'kẹt' means stuck or busy with something unavoidable; very common in Southern speech to explain a sudden schedule conflict.
'qua' implies going over to someone's place nearby; 'ăn cơm' literally means eat rice but refers to having a meal together.

chunks.note: 'đâu' softens the reassurance, making it sound natural and comforting rather than blunt or dismissive.
'ghé' means to stop by or visit briefly; adding 'sớm' specifies doing it early in the day.
'phụ' is the standard Southern word for helping out with a task; 'luôn' adds the sense of doing it right then too.

title: The Escaped Chicken

content.title: The Escaped Chicken

chunks.note: Literally 'chicken of whose house'. Natural spoken way to refer to an unidentified neighbor's animal.
Used when an animal breaks free from its enclosure. Very common in daily neighborhood talk.
'Rượt' is the Southern word for chase. 'Em' is used here as a younger adult addressing an older neighbor.
Reduplication adds a vivid, slightly humorous feel to the action of running without direction.

rounds.situation: You tell your older female neighbor about the chaos in the alley this morning.
rounds.vietnamese: Sáng nay con gà nhà ai xổng ra, rượt em chạy vòng vòng luôn.
rounds.translation: This morning someone's chicken got loose and chased me running around in circles.

chunks.note: Vivid physical description. 'Nóc' means roof or top surface, very natural for vehicles.
'Gáy' is specifically a rooster crowing. 'Ỏm tỏi' means loud and chaotic, adding humor.
'Xóm' is a small neighborhood or hamlet. 'Bu lại' means to swarm or gather closely out of curiosity.
Southern everyday word for watching or looking at something interesting.

rounds.vietnamese: Nó bay lên nóc xe máy, gáy ỏm tỏi làm cả xóm bu lại coi.

chunks.note: A very common Southern expression for being suddenly startled or frightened. Adds dramatic humor.
'Tưởng' means thought or assumed. 'Mổ' is the specific verb for a bird pecking.
'Trúng' means to hit the target. Wearing sandals is standard daily footwear in Vietnam.
Colloquial Southern phrase meaning ruined, finished, or in big trouble. Used jokingly here.
